items.title: Tech sell-off eases as stock market support measures are deployed after AI slump – business live
items.summary:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

Late last Friday, software giant Oracle declared it has secured the capital needed to fulfill its cloud infrastructure contract with OpenAI.

The announcement, just after Wall Street closed for the week, saw Oracle describe itself as the first hyperscaler fully funded for the current artificial intelligence investment cycle.

Over the weekend Oracle posted on social media that it had secured full financing for its contracts with OpenAI. This is a $300bn arrangement whereby Oracle would finance a 5-year cloud computing arrangement for the maker of ChatGPT. This would provide large scale AI infrastructure and compute capacity to power OpenAI. Oracle then confirmed that it would post positive free cash flow in fiscal 2028.

This did not reassure all of the market, with some AI critics seizing on this statement as a sign that the lady doth protest too much, and Oracle must be in trouble. Some analysts are now convinced that Oracle relies on Nvidia to backstop this arrangement, and the risk is that without Jensen Huang at the helm, the deal could fall through. This would leave Oracle on the hook to finance $300bn in a rising interest rate environment, or face a costly break clause from its contract with OpenAI.

For some markets, we could say it now. AI frenzy seemingly created a bubble and the bubble has burst. Last week was a very ugly week for the AI complex, sending many markets into the correction/bear market zone.

Among them, the South Korean…
items.t: Tech sell-off eases as stock market support measures are deployed after AI slump – business live

items.title: How Luana Lopes Lara built Kalshi into a $40 billion prediction market giant that overtook Polymarket
items.summary:
It’s Election Night 2026. Luana Lopes Lara has been preparing for this evening for at least three years. Fresh off a plane from the buttoned-up Futures Industry Association’s expo in Chicago, the 30-year-old on-paper billionaire heads straight to the downtown Manhattan offices of Kalshi, the $40 billion prediction market startup she cofounded that promises to change how we interact with the financial system and understand our future.

“Are the odds going to be everywhere? Are we going to have the best product?” Lopes Lara asks.

Her staff are waiting in a war room ready to order pizza, screens lighting up with constantly changing blue-and-red odds, a second-by-second accounting of all the trades on the Kalshi app. Will Democrats take the Senate? Kalshi’s market on that yes-or-no question is judging the odds at 76% yes, with more than $338 million collectively bet on the outcome. The Texas governor’s race market flips for underdog Democrat Gina Hinojosa, and someone screams—Lopes Lara and her team all huddle around to see what’s happened.

Kalshi and its competitor Polymarket provide an experience somewhere between betting on DraftKings and browsing X. Users put money down on any number of questions—Will the Buffalo Bills beat the Minnesota Vikings? Will Taylor Swift be seen with ex-friend Blake Lively by the end of the year? Will the price of Bitcoin increase in the next 15 minutes?— and receive a payout (or lose their money) when the answer is revealed, if they don’t cash out sooner. The technical term for these bets is an “event contract,” a form of trading regulated by…
items.t: How Luana Lopes Lara built Kalshi into a $40 billion prediction market giant that overtook Polymarket

items.title: Dodging space junk costs $58 million a year. Meet the Space Force contractor who made ‘autopilot for satellites’ to save money for taxpayers
items.summary:
Every time a satellite swerves around a piece of space junk, it can burn about $1 million worth of fuel, according to NASA . Across U.S. satellites, NASA says the cost of debris is about $58 million a year, most of it borne by military and civil spacecraft that taxpayers pay for.

That is what BQP—a Syracuse, N.Y., simulation company that began in India in 2020 and now works for the Space Force—is trying to solve. Earth orbit is filling up faster than Washington can decide who should police it. BQP says its software, which founder and CEO Abhishek Chopra calls “autopilot for satellites,” can cut that bill by letting spacecraft decide on their own when to move.

“It’s completed the ground testing successfully,” Chopra said of a test on a partner company’s hardware. “It’s actually flying to International Space Station to be tested in the real space environment.”

Abhishek Chopra, CEO of BQP. Courtesy of BQP 

A crowded orbit 

There’s a long history of spacecraft turning into trash—and authorities trying to enforce some accountability.

When NASA’s Skylab space station crashed over Western Australia in 1979, the Shire of Esperance fined the agency $400 for littering, but NASA never paid. And bills have only gotten bigger. In 1978, a Soviet satellite, Cosmos 954, scattered radioactive debris across Canada’s Northwest Territories. Canada billed Moscow about 6 million Canadian dollars and settled for 3 million. But the FCC didn’t fine a company over space debris until 2023, when it charged Dish Network $150,000 for parking a dead satellite in the wrong orbit.

Air travel faced…
items.t: Dodging space junk costs $58 million a year. Meet the Space Force contractor who made ‘autopilot for satellites’ to save money for taxpayers

items.title: Tokyo won’t fall as hard as Seoul or Taipei when the AI trade cools, says Japan Exchange Group CEO Hiromi Yamaji
items.summary:
Global AI stocks sold off sharply over the past week, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO and tighter rules around semiconductor exports. Not even Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO on Thursday revived sentiment. Tech-heavy indices fell sharply: the Nasdaq 100 fell 9.1% last week, while the PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index is down by 13% over the same period. 

Yet Hiromi Yamaji, CEO of the Japan Exchange Group (JPX), isn’t too worried about the tech turmoil hitting Japan too hard. 

“The weight of AI or semiconductor-related stocks in the TOPIX is only 11.3%… in the S&P 500 it’s 20%, in the Nasdaq100 it’s 27%, in Taiwan it’s 47%, and in Korea it’s 60%,” Yamaji tells Fortune . “If there is much less trading volume of AI-related stocks, then we will see some decrease in trading value, but the impact won’t be as much as in other markets.”

The TOPIX index, which covers the broader Japanese equity market and was developed by JPX, fell 7% last week. Japan’s other benchmark index, the Nikkei 225, dropped by 8% over the same period. (The Nikkei 225, developed by Nikkei Inc., tracks a smaller number of large Japanese companies, including more tech manufacturing companies).

Taiwan’s TAIEX index—where chipmaker TSMC makes up over 40% of the weight—crashed by 13% last week, prompting the island’s government to take measures against short-selling on Thursday to stabilize markets.

Japanese equities hit historic highs in the summer of 2026 following a series of corporate governance reforms Yamaji launched, which were aimed at improving market transparency and fairness. The…
items.t: Tokyo won’t fall as hard as Seoul or Taipei when the AI trade cools, says Japan Exchange Group CEO Hiromi Yamaji

items.title: Dow futures jump 800 points and Nasdaq soars nearly 3% as stocks rebound from correction with Wall Street still upbeat on 2027
items.summary:
Investors are poised to begin a short trading week with some early holiday cheer after suffering the worst loss in more than six years.

Futures tied to the Dow Jones industrial average surged 798 points, or 1.66%. S&P 500 futures shot up 2.11%, and Nasdaq futures soared 2.75%.

That came after the Dow and Nasdaq notched their biggest weekly declines since the early days of the COVID-10 pandemic, while the S&P 500 saw its steepest such drop since April 2025, when President Donald Trump stunned markets with his “Liberation Day” tariffs.

The S&P 500 and Dow joined the Nasdaq in correction territory. Tech shares have led the selloff as Wall Street fears the AI boom is about to go bust. The downtrend began after the midterm elections handed victories to Democrats more skeptical of data centers.

But the Nvidia spy scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s ouster as CEO poured more fuel on the fire, igniting additional worries that his “circular” financing deals would unravel and leave neocloud companies in its ecosystem without capital for new data centers or AI chips.

In addition, revelations that China had backdoor access to high-end U.S. chips used in AI development are spurring a federal crackdown to close loopholes in export restrictions. Trump even vowed to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad.

Moody’s Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi warned in a social media post that the stock market selloff could weigh on economic growth via the wealth effect, which affects consumer spending.

He estimated that that consumer spending rises or falls by about 2 cents…
items.t: Dow futures jump nearly 700 points and Nasdaq soars 3% as stocks rebound from correction with Wall Street still upbeat on 2027

items.title: Florida slashed property taxes. Now cities must cut services and ‘niceties’ like Christmas parades: ‘this is only the beginning of the vast reduction’
items.summary:
The cold reality of cutting local tax revenue by billions of dollars a year is starting to dawn on Floridians, who voted to slash property taxes earlier this month. 

Amendment 3 expands the so-called homestead exemption, shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation. It will nearly triple from $51,400 currently to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. 

It also lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% hike to 5%. The amendment doesn’t apply to school-related property taxes but creates a path for abolishing non-school property taxes completely.

State economists have projected that local governments will lose nearly $5 billion in the first year and nearly $12 billion a year once the exemption is fully phased in.

To be sure, local governments can raise revenue in other ways, such sales taxes and fees. Big cities can also rely more on taxes aimed at tourists, but smaller communities will be hit especially hard with some losing the bulk of their tax base.

Cities are now scrambling to figure out how to fund vital services like police, fire fighters and paramedics as well as roads and other infrastructure with much smaller budgets.

In Deltona, City Manager Doc Dougherty told residents that the Christmas parade was canceled and blamed Amendment 3, warning that cuts wouldn’t end there. He estimated the city’s budget must be cut by $12 million in the coming year and then another $5 million the following year. By 2030, Deltona is expected to cut more than $23 million.

items.title: Ronald Reagan said you can achieve anything—if you don’t care who gets the credit. Abdul El-Sayed channels that wisdom with ‘TrumpCare for all’
items.summary:
The Democratic legislative agenda is taking shape, and healthcare is at the top as rising medical expenses were a major driver of midterm election messaging about affordability.

But while Democrats will hold commanding majorities in the House and Senate when the new Congress convenes in January, President Donald Trump has reminded them that he is ready to veto legislation he doesn’t like.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed—a former Detroit health official who campaigned on Medicare for all—sees a way around that by appealing to Trump’s ego. On Nov. 12, he posted to social media a picture of a notional, gold-colored “TrumpCare” card, saying “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

The next day, El-Sayed doubled down, assuring CNN in an interview that he wasn’t joking and insisting that he doesn’t care what the public insurance program called.

“What you call it is secondary,” he added. “What it does in your life, that’s the whole point. None of us ran to name things, except for Donald Trump. Most of us ran to actually solve problems in people’s lives.”

That got Trump’s attention. And on Saturday, he reposted on his Truth Social account El-Sayed’s initial Nov. 12 appeal. El-Sayed posted “Let’s get to work, then.”

The gambit echoes a famous line from President Ronald Reagan in February 1988, when he spoke at a meeting of the White House Conference for a Drug Free America:

“On my desk in the Oval Office, I have a little sign that says: There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the…
items.t: Ronald Reagan said you can achieve anything—if you don’t care who gets the credit. Abdul El-Sayed channels that wisdom with ‘TrumpCare for all’

items.title: High-end genealogy travel is booming, offering luxe journeys to the roots of your family tree
items.summary:
My great-great-grandfather came to the Tuscan ghost island of Pianosa as a prisoner. I arrived there on a luxury vacation.

The island lives up to its name, I thought as my ferry drifted toward the sole dock on this protected isola fantasma . “Pianosa” is derived from piano , Italian for “flat,” and indeed the island crouches low to the cyan Tyrrhenian Sea , its shores fringed by parasol pines and deserted prison watchtowers. From 1856 to 1998, Pianosa was a remote penal colony—and the place where my ancestor, Salvatore Giovanni Pellegrino Irace, died.

I’d learned this family lore thanks to a partnership between Ancestry, the Blackstone-owned leader in the at-home DNA-testing space, and Kensington, a bespoke travel outfitter, which invited me to test-drive its Personal Heritage Journey. After I submitted a DNA sample, Ancestry got to work filling in my Italian family tree, with researchers combing archives in Tuscany, Molise, and Campania. “So the interesting thing about Salvatore,” genealogist Kyle Betit said on our initial call, “is that he died in prison of tuberculosis in 1894—and we don’t know why he was there.”

Who doesn’t love a good family mystery? That’s part of what draws clients to Kensington’s genealogical-based trips. The journeys average $20,000 to $25,000 per person, with the company’s travel desk handling all the details in high style.

San Gennaro, the 
main church in Praiano, on the Amalfi Coast. Adam Erace for Fortune

items.title: She was a go-to Manhattan babysitter as a teen. Now she’s running a $100 million-a-year AI startup whose clients include the billionaire Koch family
items.summary:
From a nationwide FAA ground stop to Microsoft and Chase outages that disrupted millions of customers, a string of recent technology failures has highlighted the need to modernize aging infrastructure while raising new fears about the risks of an increasingly AI-dependent world.

But for Jaclyn Rice Nelson, cofounder and CEO of Tribe AI, that tension is exactly why businesses should embrace the technology—not run from it.

“I don’t think that anxiety around AI is unwarranted. I think it’s very real,” Nelson told Fortune .

“[AI] is ours to shape,” Nelson said. “And the only way you can shape it is if you understand it, and the only way you understand it is if you use it—and use it a lot.”

Nelson, 41, has built her business around helping companies do just that. Founded in 2019, Tribe AI has grown to a $100 million annual run rate by helping organizations—from Fortune 500s like Hyatt and MetLife to multibillion-dollar private conglomerates like Koch Inc.—put AI to work.

Tribe said on Nov. 18 that its annualized revenue had crossed $100 million, up 3.8 times from a year earlier, as more clients moved AI projects out of the pilot stage. “The hard part is getting AI into production inside a complex business,” Nelson said in the announcement.

Before building an AI startup, Nelson learned the value of hard work as a babysitter—and later at Google 

Nelson’s instinct to build something of her own predates the AI boom by decades.

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…
items.t: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

items.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
items.summary:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage
items.t: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial

items.title: Alibaba and Tencent put their faith in Chinese chips as U.S. curbs threatens to slow down their AI development
items.summary:
Tencent and Alibaba said this week that domestic chips can cushion their cloud businesses from new U.S. restrictions on access to advanced AI processors, yet acknowledged that they could still slow the development of new AI models. 

Both tech giants reported earnings after the U.S. Department of Commerce released an interim rule expanding export controls on Monday, making them some of the first Chinese corporate responses to the restrictions. 

Chipmakers and exporters now need a license to sell advanced chips to data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The rule also requires a license for large data centers to offer substantial computing power to Chinese customers. Together, the measures are likely to restrict the amount of computing power available to Chinese companies like Alibaba and Tencent as they develop AI models and offer them to users.

Tencent 

Tencent executives, in the company’s earnings call, drew a distinction between the computing power needed to train new models and running existing ones.

“We actually don’t see an impact because our cloud business today is primarily running inference,” James Mitchell, Tencent’s chief strategy officer, told analysts on Wednesday. (Inference is the running of AI models, as opposed to training them.)

Mitchell added that Tencent had reached a stage where the inference could run on what he called a “surprisingly limited number” of domestically produced chips.

items.t: Alibaba and Tencent put their faith in Chinese chips as U.S. curbs threatens to slow down their AI development

items.title: Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy
items.summary:
Good morning. Intuit is unwinding its biggest acquisition while betting AI can help it win customers without owning the marketing platform it once viewed as central to that effort.

The QuickBooks and TurboTax parent announced Thursday it plans to sell Mailchimp, an email marketing automation platform, to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, subject to approval, with proceeds earmarked for fiscal 2027 share repurchases. Intuit paid approximately $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021. Mailchimp’s quarterly revenue fell 1% to $313 million.

Sasan Goodarzi, CEO of Intuit ( No. 231 on the Fortune 500) said on the earnings call that Intuit still wants to help businesses manage lead-to-cash needs, but believes it can do so more effectively by building AI-powered capabilities into QuickBooks rather than owning Mailchimp.

Mailchimp sale marks strategic shift 

The divestiture adds another dimension to what CFO Sandeep Aujla has called Intuit’s “reset to reaccelerate” strategy launched in August: accepting some near-term pressure on revenue per customer to rebuild customer acquisition. The strategy includes lower upfront revenue per TurboTax customer as Intuit seeks faster customer growth.

The latest results offered evidence of operating momentum. For the fiscal first quarter ended Oct. 31, revenue rose 12% to $4.35 billion, while adjusted earnings per share increased 56% to $2.91. Both exceeded analyst expectations.

In my conversation with Aujla, he pointed to mid-market revenue growth of 41% and customer growth of 30% as…
items.t: Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy
